power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .679 ", "p = .728", "p = .316", "p = .790", "p = .757"), Sentence = c("Vegetarian portions were similar in size to meat portions (-1.4 g, 95% CI -8.0 to +5.2, p = .679 on average portion weight of 378 g), underscoring that the spending difference reflects the lower price rather than a change in the quantity taken.", "Transactions including the vegetarian buffet were no more likely to include an additional product (-0.28 pp, 95% CI -1.83 to +1.28, p = .728) or an unhealthy add-on (-0.72 pp, 95% CI -2.13 to +0.69, p = .316), and involved no more add-on spending (-0.06 DKK, 95% CI -0.48 to +0.37, p = .790) compared to meat buffet transactions.", "Transactions including the vegetarian buffet were no more likely to include an additional product (-0.28 pp, 95% CI -1.83 to +1.28, p = .728) or an unhealthy add-on (-0.72 pp, 95% CI -2.13 to +0.69, p = .316), and involved no more add-on spending (-0.06 DKK, 95% CI -0.48 to +0.37, p = .790) compared to meat buffet transactions.", "Transactions including the vegetarian buffet were no more likely to include an additional product (-0.28 pp, 95% CI -1.83 to +1.28, p = .728) or an unhealthy add-on (-0.72 pp, 95% CI -2.13 to +0.69, p = .316), and involved no more add-on spending (-0.06 DKK, 95% CI -0.48 to +0.37, p = .790) compared to meat buffet transactions.", "The intervention had no detectable effect on the overall likelihood of purchasing an add-on (-0.15 pp, 95% CI -1.13 to +0.82, p = .757); however, as the event study for this outcome indicates pre-intervention divergence, we cannot say with certainty that there was no effect of the intervention." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Price interventions are proposed to promote sustainable diets, yet real-world spillover effects are rarely tested.
In three university canteens (94,740 transactions), one lowered vegetarian and increased meat buffet prices for 15 weeks.
Unhealthy add-on purchases fell 1.09 percentage points relative to controls, a 26% relative reduction.
Cheaper vegetarian lunches involved comparable portions and no more add-ons than meat lunches.
We find no evidence that price differentiation shifts unhealthy consumption elsewhere.
Meat consumption is among the leading contributors to global greenhouse gas emissions (GHGs) and biodiversity loss [1] [2] [3] .
text.formatted: Meat consumption is among the leading contributors to global greenhouse gas emissions (GHGs) and biodiversity loss <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> .

text.text: Diets lower in meat are associated with lower environmental impacts and broadly consistent with dietary guidelines, suggesting that environmental and health benefits may coincide 4 .
text.formatted: Diets lower in meat are associated with lower environmental impacts and broadly consistent with dietary guidelines, suggesting that environmental and health benefits may coincide <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Monetary incentives, such as taxation or subsidies, are widely promoted and considered an important policy lever for promoting more sustainable diets 4 .
text.formatted: Monetary incentives, such as taxation or subsidies, are widely promoted and considered an important policy lever for promoting more sustainable diets <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Targeted changes in value added tax (VAT), increasing VAT on meat and dairy while reducing it on fruits and vegetables, are projected to deliver simultaneous environmental, economic, and health gains.

Yet policy measures that alter incentive structures can generate indirect effects beyond their primary target 5 -both negative, in the form of rebound effects or negative spillovers 6, 7 , and positive, in the form of co-benefits.
text.formatted: Yet policy measures that alter incentive structures can generate indirect effects beyond their primary target <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> -both negative, in the form of rebound effects or negative spillovers <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> , and positive, in the form of co-benefits.

text.text: Some modelling work suggests these benefits may be partially offset 8 , i.e., meat taxation could increase sugar consumption, limiting its health co-benefits.
text.formatted: Some modelling work suggests these benefits may be partially offset <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , i.e., meat taxation could increase sugar consumption, limiting its health co-benefits.

text.text: More broadly, modelling studies dominate the evidence on how consumers respond to meat-related price interventions 4, [8] [9] [10] which limits our understanding of the broader impacts of these policies.
text.formatted: More broadly, modelling studies dominate the evidence on how consumers respond to meat-related price interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> which limits our understanding of the broader impacts of these policies.

text.text: It is therefore imperative to investigate the potential unintended consequences of pricing differentiation in real-world settings 11.
text.formatted: It is therefore imperative to investigate the potential unintended consequences of pricing differentiation in real-world settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref>.

text.text: Here we present a quasi-experimental study testing a price-based intervention to promote sustainable food purchases in university canteens.

Specifically, we examine whether differentiated buffet pricing -increasing the cost of a meat-containing lunch buffet while decreasing the cost of a vegetarian alternative -generates positive or negative spillover effects across economic and health dimensions.
We obtained anonymous transaction data from three university canteens over the period August 26, 2024, to December 2025, covering 94,740 analyzed transactions.
Across all three canteens, students and employees can purchase a buffet lunch priced by weight, with vegetarian and meat options available.

From August 25, 2025, to December 2025, one canteen (the treatment canteen) introduced differentiated pricing; the vegetarian buffet price was reduced by 1.5 DKK/100 g, and the meat buffet price increased by 1.5 DKK/100 g (a 3.0 DKK/100 g spread, ≈ €0.40).
The two other canteens (control canteens) maintained undifferentiated pricing throughout.

Two existing cashier stations were designated for vegetarian and meat buffet purchases, respectively, enabling transaction-level classification of buffet type during the intervention period (see Supplementary Fig. 1 for visualization of the set-up).
text.formatted: Two existing cashier stations were designated for vegetarian and meat buffet purchases, respectively, enabling transaction-level classification of buffet type during the intervention period (see Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for visualization of the set-up).

text.text: To assess the unintended effects of the intervention, we examine (1) whether customers selecting the vegetarian option spent less overall; (2) whether they were more or less likely to purchase additional (un)healthy products alongside their meal; and (3) whether, relative to the control canteens, unhealthy add-on purchasing changed in the treatment canteen during the intervention period.

All analyses use linear probability models for binary outcomes and OLS regression for continuous outcomes, with day-of-week and month included as fixed effects to isolate daily and seasonal variation in purchasing behavior from the predictor.
Standard errors were clustered by year-week in all models to account for correlation among transactions occurring in the same week.

To assess health outcomes, all additional products purchased alongside the buffet were classified by Nutri-Score 12 , with products scoring C, D and E, e.g., sweetened drinks, pastry or chocolate bars, classified as unhealthy.
text.formatted: To assess health outcomes, all additional products purchased alongside the buffet were classified by Nutri-Score <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> , with products scoring C, D and E, e.g., sweetened drinks, pastry or chocolate bars, classified as unhealthy.

text.text: During the intervention period, 60.9% of buffet transactions in the treatment canteen were vegetarian (see Fig. 1).
text.formatted: During the intervention period, 60.9% of buffet transactions in the treatment canteen were vegetarian (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: As it was not possible to distinguish between meat and vegetarian buffet before the intervention period, the canteen procurement data were used to capture the change in meat demand.

Meat-related emissions, controlled for the amount of food purchased by the canteen before and after the intervention, within the same period of the year (the fall semester, i.e., September to December 2024 and 2025), declined in the treated canteen by 7.3 %.

In the treatment canteen during the intervention (N = 6,294), transactions including the vegetarian buffet involved 10.66 DKK less total spending compared to transactions including the meat buffet (95% CI -11.65 to -9.68, p < .001; mean 35.06 vs 45.62 DKK).
text.formatted: In the treatment canteen during the intervention (N = 6,294), transactions including the vegetarian buffet involved 10.66 DKK less total spending compared to transactions including the meat buffet (95% CI -11.65 to -9.68, p < .001; mean 35.06 vs 45.62 DKK).

text.text: Vegetarian portions were similar in size to meat portions (-1.4 g, 95% CI -8.0 to +5.2, p = .679 on average portion weight of 378 g), underscoring that the spending difference reflects the lower price rather than a change in the quantity taken.

Transactions including the vegetarian buffet were no more likely to include an additional product (-0.28 pp, 95% CI -1.83 to +1.28, p = .728) or an unhealthy add-on (-0.72 pp, 95% CI -2.13 to +0.69, p = .316), and involved no more add-on spending (-0.06 DKK, 95% CI -0.48 to +0.37, p = .790) compared to meat buffet transactions.
However, because buffet choice was not random, this evidence is correlational.
Within the limits of what is observable in a single transaction, we find no indication that the money saved by choosing the cheaper option was redirected toward additional food, snacks, or drink.
To address potential self-selection bias, we also estimated the effect of the intervention itself on additional product purchases using a difference-in-differences (DiD) design.
We compared the changes in purchasing behavior over time in the treatment canteen relative to the control canteens, with canteen, month, and day-of-week fixed effects.

The parallel trends assumption, critical for the validity of the DiD analysis, was investigated using visual inspection of weekly series (Supplementary Fig. 3), an event study 13 (Supplementary Fig. 4), and a placebo test assigning the intervention date within the pre-intervention period (Supplementary Tab 2).
text.formatted: The parallel trends assumption, critical for the validity of the DiD analysis, was investigated using visual inspection of weekly series (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">3</ref>), an event study <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">4</ref>), and a placebo test assigning the intervention date within the pre-intervention period (Supplementary Tab 2).

text.text: For unhealthy purchasing, all three checks were consistent with parallel trends.
For general add-on purchasing, two preintervention event-study coefficients differed from the reference period, indicating weaker support for the parallel trends' assumption.
The effect of intervention on additional purchases is displayed in Fig. 2.
text.formatted: The effect of intervention on additional purchases is displayed in Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>.

text.text: The intervention had no detectable effect on the overall likelihood of purchasing an add-on (-0.15 pp, 95% CI -1.13 to +0.82, p = .757); however, as the event study for this outcome indicates pre-intervention divergence, we cannot say with certainty that there was no effect of the intervention.

Contrary to expectations, it reduced the probability of purchasing an unhealthy add-on by 1.09 percentage points (95% CI -1.90 to -0.28, p = .009), a 26% reduction relative to the pre-intervention rate of 4.21%.

Unhealthy add-on purchasing declined at all three canteens over this period (-1.34, -0.46, and -0.16 pp at the treatment and two control canteens, respectively); the estimate above reflects the difference in these changes.

The effect was robust to dropping either of the two control canteens (-0.89 pp, p = .026, and -1.31 pp, p = .006) and to a stricter threshold counting only Nutri-Score D and E products as unhealthy (-0.94 pp, 95% CI -1.61 to -0.27, p = .006).

Because treatment was assigned to a single canteen, we additionally report studentized randomization inference 14, 15 by reassigning the intervention date to each of 30 weeks within the treatment canteen (p = .032, the minimum achievable value given the length of the preintervention period allowing for 30 placebo tests corresponding to 0 placebos producing the observed effect).
text.formatted: Because treatment was assigned to a single canteen, we additionally report studentized randomization inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> by reassigning the intervention date to each of 30 weeks within the treatment canteen (p = .032, the minimum achievable value given the length of the preintervention period allowing for 30 placebo tests corresponding to 0 placebos producing the observed effect).

text.text: These findings indicate that the intervention was accompanied by a reduction in the purchase of unhealthy add-on products.
Difference-in-differences coefficients (circles) with 95% confidence intervals, estimated by OLS with canteen, month and day-of-week fixed effects and standard errors clustered by year-week.
The outcome is the probability that a buffet transaction includes an add-on product, so coefficients are in percentage points.

The sample comprises 94,740 buffet transactions across three university canteens and three semesters; one canteen introduced differentiated buffet pricing for 15 weeks during the autumn 2025 semester.
Red denotes unhealthy add-on purchases under the primary Nutri-Score C-E classification, purple the stricter D-E classification, and grey any add-on purchase irrespective of Nutri-Score.
Lighter rows beneath each estimate show the same model re-estimated, dropping each control canteen in turn (Control 1 and Control 2).

RI p shows randomization inference, in which the intervention date was reassigned to each of 30 weeks in the treatment canteen's pre-intervention period; its minimum achievable value is .032, so significance thresholds are not applied here. * p < .05; ** p < .01; *** p < .001.
text.formatted: RI p shows randomization inference, in which the intervention date was reassigned to each of 30 weeks in the treatment canteen's pre-intervention period; its minimum achievable value is .032, so significance thresholds are not applied here. * p < .05; ** p < .01; *** p < .001.

text.text: Contrary to evidence that meat taxation can increase sugar consumption and thereby limit health co-benefits 8 , we found no evidence of negative spillover effects from the price differentiation between meat and vegetarian buffet options.
text.formatted: Contrary to evidence that meat taxation can increase sugar consumption and thereby limit health co-benefits <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , we found no evidence of negative spillover effects from the price differentiation between meat and vegetarian buffet options.

text.text: Instead, our findings provide real-world support for modelling studies projecting health and economic cobenefits from price-based meat interventions 4, 16 : transactions including the cheaper vegetarian buffet involved lower total spending for the entire basket, with no indication that customers redirected their savings toward additional purchases.
text.formatted: Instead, our findings provide real-world support for modelling studies projecting health and economic cobenefits from price-based meat interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> : transactions including the cheaper vegetarian buffet involved lower total spending for the entire basket, with no indication that customers redirected their savings toward additional purchases.

text.text: At the canteen level, the intervention was accompanied by an overall reduction in unhealthy purchasing.
Our study contributes to the literature on behavioral spillover effects.

During the intervention period, the university's efforts to reduce GHG emissions and the role of meat consumption in this initiative were clearly communicated in the treatment canteen (see Supplementary Fig. 2).
text.formatted: During the intervention period, the university's efforts to reduce GHG emissions and the role of meat consumption in this initiative were clearly communicated in the treatment canteen (see Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: This communication context may have contributed to the observed positive spillover effect, which research suggests is more likely when the rationale behind an intervention is made explicit rather than framed as a purely economic incentive 17, 18.
text.formatted: This communication context may have contributed to the observed positive spillover effect, which research suggests is more likely when the rationale behind an intervention is made explicit rather than framed as a purely economic incentive <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref>.

text.text: Despite the positive outlook offered by these results, they should be interpreted with some caution.
Our study focuses on the food-related domain at a university canteen; potential spillover effects in other sustainability domains, such as transportation, warrant further investigation.
We also cannot rule out the possibility that negative spillovers emerge with a time delay or outside the canteen setting.
Our data also do not allow us to separate the price-based intervention from the communication about the intervention.
Furthermore, these results do not provide causal evidence about the effectiveness of price-based measures on meat sales, as this has been investigated elsewhere 19, 20.
text.formatted: Furthermore, these results do not provide causal evidence about the effectiveness of price-based measures on meat sales, as this has been investigated elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref>.

text.text: The study was approved by the Institutional Ethical Review Board, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science (approval number SODAS-2025-012), in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (1964) and its subsequent amendments.
Data analyzed in the presented study were collected by the canteen provider and were anonymized prior to their delivery to the research team.
The transaction and procurement data were analyzed only in anonymized, aggregate form; individual informed consent for secondary research use was accordingly not obtained.
The customers were notified about the ongoing research via posters located in the canteens during the intervention period.

From a canteen provider, we obtained anonymous transaction data from three university canteens from August 26, 2024, to December 2025, covering 137,389 buffet transactions in total (treated canteen n = 42,880, control canteen 1 n = 45,812, control canteen 2 n = 48,697).
After data cleaning, 94,740 (treated canteen n = 27,371, control canteen 1 n = 30,401, control canteen 2 n = 36,968) valid buffet transactions were identified.
A buffet transaction was classified as any individual transaction in one of the three canteens that contained a purchase of a lunch buffet.

Before the analysis, the data were inspected, and invalid transactions were excluded; specifically, (1) negative transactions corresponding to refunds and (2) transactions containing more than one buffet purchase (i.e., purchases for several customers) were removed.
Across all canteens, weeks with irregular activity, i.e., canteen closures or school vacation (summer, week 42, weeks 51-52), were excluded, resulting in 53 weeks of observation period.
All three canteens included in this study are located in Copenhagen, Denmark, and are part of one faculty of a large university and are catered by the same canteen provider.
All three canteens are similar in size (with a similar level of daily buffet transactions) and have the same buffet system with pricing based on weight, but they are in different parts of the city.
Across all three canteens, students and employees can purchase a buffet lunch priced by weight, with both vegetarian and meat options available.

From August 25, 2025 to December 2025, one canteen (the treatment canteen) introduced differentiated pricing: the vegetarian buffet price was reduced by 1.5 DKK/100 g and the meat buffet price increased by 1.5 DKK/100 g (a 3.0 DKK/100 g spread, ≈ €0.40); the two remaining canteens (control canteens) maintained undifferentiated pricing throughout.
Two cashier stations operated in the treatment canteen throughout the study period and were not moved or added to at any point.

From week 35 of 2025 until the end of December 2025, these two existing stations were designated for vegetarian and meat buffet purchases, respectively, enabling transaction-level classification of buffet type.
Both stations were located adjacent to the buffet, with the fridge and snack shelves approximately 3 m away; this configuration was unchanged across the pre-intervention and intervention periods.
Therefore, the vegetarian and meat buffet distinction is possible only in the treatment canteen during the intervention period.
Individual transaction data were obtained from the canteen provider for the purposes of this study.

Each observation represents a single transaction recorded at one of the three canteen locations, including timestamp, buffet purchase, additional food and beverage items, and paid price for each item.
Spending for lunch buffet was calculated as the total amount paid for the transaction, including any additional items.
A transaction was classified as containing an add-on (binary) when it included a buffet purchase together with at least one additional food or beverage item.
Packaging materials, deposit items, and other non-food products were excluded from this classification to ensure that only additional purchases intended for consumption were considered.
Each product was assigned a Nutri-Score to classify its nutritional quality using the Nutri-Score scale ranging from A (healthiest) to E (least healthy) 12 .
text.formatted: Each product was assigned a Nutri-Score to classify its nutritional quality using the Nutri-Score scale ranging from A (healthiest) to E (least healthy) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Out of 131 unique products, 98 products were classified as unhealthy.
See Supplementary Tab 1 for full list.
All buffet transactions with add-ons classified as C, D, or E were labelled as unhealthy purchases (binary).
As a robustness check, we also applied a stricter classification, labelling only products classified as D and E (68 unique products) as unhealthy.

Nutri-Score classification was manually calculated using the 2024 Nutri-Score algorithm 12 applied to nutritional composition data obtained from retailer websites, or, in the case of unbranded products (e.g., homemade croissant), from the nutritional information indicated for similar products in The Danish Food Composition Database 21.
text.formatted: Nutri-Score classification was manually calculated using the 2024 Nutri-Score algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> applied to nutritional composition data obtained from retailer websites, or, in the case of unbranded products (e.g., homemade croissant), from the nutritional information indicated for similar products in The Danish Food Composition Database <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, monthly procurement data including the list of products purchased, their quantity, and corresponding CO₂ data per category per weight (calculated according to the GHG Protocol 22 ) provided by the canteen provider.
text.formatted: Additionally, monthly procurement data including the list of products purchased, their quantity, and corresponding CO₂ data per category per weight (calculated according to the GHG Protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> ) provided by the canteen provider.

text.text: The procurement data were used to calculate the change in meat-related CO₂ before and after the intervention, within the same period of the year (fall semester 2024 and 2025) by aggregating the CO 2 emissions and kg of food purchased during each period.
However, due to the missing control condition, the reported decline in CO2 emissions should not be interpreted as a causal impact of the intervention.
All analyses were conducted in Python.

Regression models using buffet type (meat vs vegetarian) with month and day-of-week fixed effects were used to separate the effect of selecting the cheaper vegetarian meal from specific day of the week and seasonality, e.g., the exam period in the treated canteen during the intervention.

Difference-indifferences (DiD) models included canteen, month, and day-of-week fixed effects to estimate the differential change in purchasing behavior in the treated canteen compared to control canteens.
Seasonality was captured with month and not a week, because the 53-week clusters were insufficient to support reliable cluster-robust inference with week-of-year fixed effects.
In all models, the standard errors were clustered by year-week to account for the dependency between transactions in the same week.

We assessed the parallel trends assumption with an event study, visual inspection of weekly series (Supplementary Fig. 3), and a placebo test assigning a false intervention date within the pre-intervention period (Supplementary Table 2).
text.formatted: We assessed the parallel trends assumption with an event study, visual inspection of weekly series (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">3</ref>), and a placebo test assigning a false intervention date within the pre-intervention period (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: For unhealthy purchasing, all three were consistent with parallel trends; for any general add-on purchasing, the event study indicated pre-treatment divergence.
Because the design contains a single treated unit, common in applied policy settings, we additionally report randomization inference following MacKinnon and Webb 15 .
text.formatted: Because the design contains a single treated unit, common in applied policy settings, we additionally report randomization inference following MacKinnon and Webb <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Cluster-robust t-tests substantially overreject when the number of treated clusters is small; randomization inference addresses this issue.
We reassigned the intervention date to each of 30 weeks in the pre-intervention period at the treatment canteen, excluding the first and last four weeks.
The weeks before the assigned date were treated as pre-intervention and weeks after were treated as post-intervention.
We re-estimated the model and compared the t-statistic to the observed estimates.

The randomization p-value is computed as (1 + k)/(1 + n), where k is the number of placebo assignments at least as extreme as the observed estimate; the minimum achievable value is therefore 1/31 = .032.

We did not reassign treatment status across all canteens, because placebo estimates from the control canteens are centered away from zero (-0.87 and +0.41 pp), indicating that the canteens are not exchangeable under the null (for details see Supplementary Tab 3).
This exchangeability concern is distinct from the parallel trends assumption, as it concerns permuting which unit is treated, not the intervention date within a fixed treated unit.
Finally, to confirm that results were not driven by idiosyncratic changes at either control canteen, we re-estimated all models dropping each control in turn.
